17.0.0.en: 1 The Lord created man of the earth, 2 and turned him into it again. 3 He gave them a set time and numbered days, and gave them authority over all that is in it, and clothed them with strength according to their nature, and made them in His own image. 4 He cast the fear of him upon all flesh, and gave him dominion over beast and bird. 5 He created from him a helper like himself, and gave them choice, and a tongue, and two eyes, and two ears, and a heart to think with, 6 and filled them with the knowledge of wisdom, and showed them good and evil.

17.1.0.en: The book highlights how greatly God cherishes man as a unique creature, very dear to Him. 1. Man was created from dust (Gen 2:7), and when he sinned he became subject to death (Gen 3:19), as the fruit of his disobedience to God, the source of his life. The book of Sirach highlights the dread of death in man's eyes, since he anticipates it at every moment of his life. But as we depart from the world we realize that it is fitting for us not to be occupied with what we lived on earth, whether one day or a thousand years, but what concerns us there is the manner of our life: were we in fellowship with God or strangers to Him? Our life is a set time, but in the age to come there is immortality in heaven, where we see God and enjoy eternal glory, or eternal deprivation of the Kingdom of Heaven. 2. Even if some animals surpass man in the size of the body, like elephants, or in physical strength, like the lion, or in speed, like the deer, or in the ability to fly, like the eagle, or to swim in the depths of the oceans, like the fish, yet God gave him authority, and the Lord cast the dread of man upon all living creatures [2-4]. 3. Man shares with many animals the possession of life, tongue, eyes and brain, and is distinguished from them in that he alone is in the image and likeness of God; God also clothed him with strength befitting the beloved of God [3] and gave him reason and free will. 4. Sometimes an animal surpasses man in the use of some of the senses in earthly matters: by smell an animal can recognize a poisonous plant, whereas man needs scientific study to realize that it contains a poisonous substance. 5. Man's senses are used to go beyond the earthly and the temporal: the tongue supports man in praising with the heavenly beings, and through the eyes the inner insight can see what is unseen. Some of the Fathers see that man's five senses can contribute to the senses of the inner man [13]. 6. The animal has a brain but has no mind to support it in development and progress, such as the study of space and electronics and the learning of the laws of nature, and even meeting with God eternally and getting to know the heavenly beings. 7. God gave man the capacity to receive free grace, which supports him in enjoying the mysteries of the divine Law, and even gives him delight in keeping it, and presents him with surpassing knowledge [7-11]. 8. God honors man, dealing with him as though an equal with an equal, entering with him into a covenant not on a temporary, temporal level but on an eternal level [12]. 9. God longs that man look to the glory of His majesty and hear the glory of His voice, because his eternal destiny is the divine embrace, where he enjoys the heavenly glories.

17.1.1.en: v Why was man created? That he might glorify God and see Him through His creation, God who brought creation into being for the sake of man.

17.1.2.en: The mind that loves God is an invisible gift which God presents for the attainment of the good life [1].

17.1.3.en: v The gravest diseases of the soul and the worst calamities and misfortunes are not knowing Him who created all things for the sake of man and gave him reason and granted him the word, by which he rises on high and has fellowship with God, contemplating and glorifying Him [2].

17.1.4.en: St. Anthony the Great The Lord created man of the earth, and turned him into it again [1].

17.1.5.en: v We heard that the Lord took "dust of the ground" and "made man" (see Gen 2:7). From this verse I became convinced that man is nothing and great at the same time. If you look at our earthly nature by itself, it is nothing and deserves nothing, but if you look at the dignity with which he was crowned, you see man to be great...

17.1.6.en: God did not say, "Let man be," as He said, "Let there be a firmament." Thus you see that man was not created like the rest of the creatures. The creation of man is higher than the light and the heaven and the heavenly bodies, indeed above everything. Our body received the dignity of being wholly fashioned by the hands of God. God did not command an angel, nor did the earth give birth to us spontaneously as it gives birth to some insects. He did not report that the angelic powers who serve Him do this or that. But with His own hand, like an artist, He took dust from the earth and formed man.

17.2.0.en: When you contemplate what the Lord took (the dust), you realize what man is. But when you contemplate Him who fashioned him, you realize that man is great. Truly, he is nothing because of the material from which he was created, and great because of the dignity he received from God his Creator [3].

17.2.1.en: St. Basil the Great Man returned to dust by his fall into rebellion against his Creator, yet the Creator did not abandon him but bore the sins of the world on the cross, and gave him the possibility of restoring the image of God by the worth of the Blood. St. Gregory of Nyssa sees that among God's blessings to man is that he is changeable: by grace he rises from glory to glory, and by negligence he falls and loses his salvation.

17.3.0.en: v Since we are changeable, it is better that we change to what is better: "from glory to glory" (2 Cor 3:18). This makes us always advance toward perfection by daily growth, without being content with certain limits on the way to perfection. That is, not stopping short of what is better, and not setting any limits at which we stop in our growth [4].

17.3.1.en: St. Gregory of Nyssa He appointed for men numbered days and a set time, and gave them authority over it [2].

17.4.0.en: St. Mar Jacob of Serugh [5] spoke of true greatness and false greatness; he spoke creatively, highlighting God's surpassing love toward man. He adorned heaven with the stars, and prepared the earth with beautiful creatures, and presented both to man to be under his authority. God wanted man to be possessor of glory and authority, but through the envy of the devil he fell into false greatness, and so lost his true greatness. Yet God allowed Adam to return to what he had been, dust, not to humiliate him, but lest he live forever having lost his greatness; rather, by discovering his true reality he obtains glory through the work of the Savior.

17.4.1.en: And clothed them with strength like His own, and made them in His own image [3].

17.5.0.en: v The Lord drew His image in us because of His compassion, and by these same mercies He will raise us up on the last day [6].

17.6.0.en: v He formed all beings in their shapes, and He drew no image of Himself except upon Adam. The earth is wide, the heaven high, the sun radiant, the moon beautiful, and the march of the hosts glorious. When He made all this beauty, it was not heard that the Lord made anything in His image, except Adam, the image of the only-begotten (Son), and for his sake he was called the image of God [7].

17.7.0.en: v God left the archangels in order to draw His image and likeness in the human soul. He adorned it with a beauty by which it surpassed all creatures [8].

17.8.0.en: v His image made them acquire boldness, so that they might supplicate Him without shame by means of His own (image) [9].

17.9.0.en: v The soul is a noble and beautiful creature, which no other creature surpasses. It is the image of the King, and the noble image of divinity, and its beauty surpasses the beauty of all creatures. Consider how beautiful was the light of the first day, yet God did not draw upon it the beautiful image of divinity. Look at the firmament, the tent stretched over all creatures; it too was not worthy to bear the image of the King, nor did the sun and the moon with their rays deserve to bear the noble image [10].

17.9.1.en: St. Mar Jacob of Serugh v St. Basil the Great says that the city of the Lord (Ps 101) is man, because God created him in His image and likeness. As for the wicked of the earth and the workers of iniquity, they are the evil thoughts that come out of the heart, such as murder, debauchery, adultery, theft, false witness, blasphemy, and the like. We must kill them and destroy them from the city of the Lord early, that is, in their beginnings or in the youth of our age, and not let them grow in us all the more.

17.9.2.en: Father Anthimus of Jerusalem v What does the Holy Bible mean when it says that we were created in the image of God?

17.9.3.en: Let us learn the things that concern God, and understand those that concern ourselves, namely that we have nothing that is in the image of God in bodily form, for the form of the body is corruptible. What is incorruptible is not described by what is corruptible, just as what is corruptible is not an image of what is incorruptible...

17.9.4.en: How, then, can what is changeable resemble what is unchangeable? Our human body flees from us like a river that flows away before we see it end. It appears in one form and then in another.

17.9.5.en: "In our image"! Do we obtain from the unchangeable nature a changeable image? Do we obtain a form from One who has no form? Then how do we examine what is according to the image? From the things which the Lord Himself spoke. If I speak something of my own, do not accept it, but if it is the word of the Lord, then truly accept it in your heart.

17.9.6.en: "Let us make man in our image, after our likeness: and let them have dominion over the fish of the sea" (Gen 1:26). Is it by the body or by the mind? Does that power of dominion lie in the spirit or in the body? The body is weaker than the animals; what comparison is there between the body of a man and the body of a camel; between a man and an ox; between a man and any wild animal you choose? The body of a man is easily captured and attacked by a beast of prey.

17.10.0.en: In what does the principle of dominion lie? In the exalted rank of the mind. What the strength of the body lacked was completed by the mind! But how can man move heavy, huge weights? By thought or by the strength of the body? [11]

17.11.0.en: St. Basil the Great v If you wish, you can be a slave to the passions. And if you wish, you can be freed from them and not submit to their yoke, for God created you and gave you this authority. Whoever conquers the passions of the body is crowned with incorruption. For if there were no passions, there could be no virtues, and consequently God would not give crowns to those who deserve them [12].

17.11.1.en: St. Anthony the Great And He cast the fear of man upon all flesh, and gave him authority over the beasts and the birds [4].

17.11.2.en: And He gave men the ability to study, and gave them a tongue and two eyes and two ears and a heart to think with [5].

17.11.3.en: Man can have a history because He created him as a storyteller; every man receives from his forebears accounts of God's work with them, and tells them in turn to the coming generations. God declared Himself to man through nature and history even before sending Moses and delivering to him the written Law.

17.12.0.en: v Those who do not see what is profitable for them, and do not look at what is good, these have blind souls and blind minds also. We must not look to them, lest through our negligence we fall into their sufferings against our will, as happens with the blind (who are led by the blind) [13].

17.13.0.en: St. Anthony the Great v I alone possess freedom from the house of creatures that glorify You by the swift course of their natures. Neither the sun nor the radiant moon nor the stars revolve swiftly in their courses by their own will. Your great power compels them all to praise You, and they do not discern their freedom in order to praise Your fear. Praise befits me, I who am free, if I understand, for my will has authority to cease from praise or to continue in it [14].

17.14.0.en: v By our will we become healthy or sick, for we are the cause of our health and our sickness [15].

17.14.1.en: St. Mar Jacob of Serugh And He filled them with skill in understanding, and showed them good and evil [6].

17.14.2.en: In a creative way St. Mar Jacob of Serugh speaks of the loftiness of the mind in the life of man, likening it, as it is in the head of man, that is, on high, to God who dwells on high, that is, in the heavens. At the same time, since the mind has its leading role with the human will in the life of man, he warns us against negligence in sanctifying it, and against deviating toward following the bodily passions that darken the mind and bring the soul down to be in bondage to the body, so that it appears as if it were bodily.

17.15.0.en: v Whoever comes to the Church does not come without discernment like the animals that have no understanding. No one visits the doctor's clinic out of mere habit, unless illness compels him to visit it seeking healing [16].

17.16.0.en: v (God) perfected the brain as a house for the mind, so that it might sit there on the upper floor like God [17].

17.17.0.en: v The mind is darkened by the passions lest it understand... Whoever overeats lowers his soul to become flesh [18].

17.17.1.en: St. Mar Jacob of Serugh And He set His eye upon their hearts, to show them the greatness of His works [7].

17.17.2.en: With all the wonderful advantages that man has enjoyed, he is nevertheless exceedingly superior by his inner man; with his heart and his inner faculties he can realize the greatness of God's work in him and with him.

17.17.3.en: So they praise His holy name, that they may fully describe the great things of His works [8].

17.17.4.en: He gave man the ability to express his pride in the wonders of God that He presents to him, by praising His holy name; for it is within the ability of man, though created from dust and living on earth, to share with the heavenly beings their praises to God.

17.18.0.en: v The soul exists in the body, and the mind exists in the soul, and the word exists in the mind, and by the word we contemplate and glorify God, who gives immortality to the soul and grants it incorruptible, eternal happiness. For God alone granted existence by the goodness of God [19].

17.18.1.en: St. Anthony the Great Since St. John Chrysostom was a preacher of the heavenly life, looking to the first work of the Lord Christ, to make heaven out of earth and angels out of men, praise is the first and chief work, whether in the life of the Church as a community or in the life of the believer as a member of it.

17.18.2.en: v Are you a craftsman? As you sit at your work, chant the psalms. Do you not want to praise with your mouth? Do it in your heart. The psalm is a great companion. You are not doing hard labor. You sit at your work as in a monastery.

17.19.0.en: v Praise is good in itself, and the psalm offers many good things: it separates the mind from the earth, and gives the soul wings, and makes (the wings) light, able to fly in the air. Therefore Paul says: "Singing and making melody in your heart to the Lord" (Eph 5:19).. There is a need for praise for the life of the psalmist and for his prayer and success [20].

17.20.0.en: v Job was crowned and became famous, not because he did not waver despite the countless trials that surrounded him, and despite his wife's opposition to him, but because he continued thanking the Lord in every state, not only when he was rich but also when he became poor, not only when he was in health but also when his body was struck (with sores), not when these things came upon him slowly, but when a violent storm came upon his house as well as upon his entire person [21].

17.21.0.en: v When the messengers came to the blessed Job, one after another, and he heard them announce deadly news, in addition to the unbearable destruction of his children, he did not cry out nor sigh, but took refuge in prayer and offered thanksgivings to the Lord. Imitate him [22].

17.22.0.en: 7 And He set His eye upon their hearts, to show them the greatness of His works. 8 That they might praise His holy name, and declare the greatness of His works. 9 And He increased them in knowledge, and made them inherit the Law of life. 10 And He made with them an everlasting covenant, and showed them His judgments. 11 So their eyes saw the greatness of glory, and their ears heard the glory of His voice.

17.23.0.en: He gave them knowledge, and gave them the Law of life as an inheritance [9].

17.23.1.en: It was within man's ability to look with the inner insight, or the heart, at the works of God and to come into contact with His surpassing care and His love for him. Man discovered that God alone sees his heart and examines it and hears his hidden voice, and man enjoys the mutual love between himself and his heavenly Beloved. Man's perception of God's work and his trust in what He prepares for him drive him to faith, which is the first channel of his enjoyment of fellowship with God. "Without faith it is impossible to please Him" (Heb 11:6). By this faith he came to know the works of God that He prepared for him to serve Him before He created him. "Through faith we understand that the worlds were framed by the word of God, so that things which are seen were not made of things which do appear" (Heb 11:3). This divine look in the human heart helped man to look to God's wisdom in the heart in all things, and gave them the knowledge of His judgments [9].

17.24.0.en: v Our eyes do not see (the moon) in the fullness of its size at all times. Now it represents the perfection of a round disc, and when it wanes and diminishes, a deficiency appears on one side. And when it increases from a crescent to a full moon, it is dark on one side. And when it is pale, the other side disappears. Now it is not without a mystical reason that the divine Creator of the universe makes the moon appear from time to time in different shapes. It is a striking example of our nature. Nothing is stable in man. Here man rises from nothing to perfection... and suddenly is subject to a gradual decline and is shattered by continual decrease. Thus looking at the moon makes us think of the swiftness of the changes of human affairs, and teaches us not to be proud of the good things of this life, nor to glory in our authority, nor to be lured by passing wealth, but rather to despise our body, which is subject to change, and to care for the soul, because its goodness is unchangeable [23].

17.24.1.en: St. Basil the Great And He established with them an everlasting covenant, and showed them His judgments [10].

17.24.2.en: So their eyes saw the greatness of His glory, and their ears heard the glory of His voice [11].

17.24.3.en: Sirach moved from the book of Genesis, where God declared Himself through nature, to the book of Exodus, where God declared Himself on Mount Sinai, where He established a covenant with His people, so that they saw His glory and heard the glory of His voice [11].

17.24.4.en: Since God created man's heart longing that God declare to him His word and His wisdom, He came through fire and mist on Mount Sinai and fulfilled the desire of man's heart, as He delivered to him the Law as a gift to His people [9].

17.24.5.en: He engraved His Law on stone and delivered it to them, as though He guarded the human heart from turning into stone. In other words, if the iniquities of mankind and all their sins had turned the human heart to stone, then through His divine fire He engraved His Law on the stone, so that man might surrender to Him his stony heart and the finger of God might engrave His Law upon it.

17.24.6.en: In the book of Genesis God created all mankind in His likeness, and in the book of Exodus God declared the establishment of His covenant with him who cleaves to Him and becomes a member of His people and accepts the renewal of his heart in order to regain the divine image.

17.24.7.en: God gave man a soul that receives His commandments, which He declares to him naturally throughout human history. Man is the only being of whom it can be said that he has an extended and advancing history. Man can perceive God's ways, which are not hidden from his eyes and from his inner insight [13]. If God requires of all the nations, as of every man: "Beware of all unrighteousness, and He gave every man commandment concerning his neighbor" [14], then all the more, in His dispensation for the salvation of the nations and of Israel, He does not allow injustice; He is a lover of all mankind, and righteous in His plan and His dispensation for the salvation of the world. This plan is summarized in the following:

17.24.8.en: First: He appointed kings and rulers for every nation, and He shepherds Israel as the portion of the Lord, and in His care He shows them no partiality.

17.24.9.en: Second: by the spirit of evil the nations were drawing Israel away and enticing it to worship idols, so both sides fell into evil. The nations enticed Israel, and Israel betrayed the Lord by worshiping the idols of the nations and committing pagan abominations.

17.24.10.en: Third: without partiality God allowed Israel to be scattered among the peoples because of its sins, and at the same time He opened for them the door of return to the Promised Land; if they repent, He gathers them from the ends of the world. 1. The goal of the commandment is that man practice love toward his brothers in humanity, so that he cannot bear to wrong his brother, and exerts all effort to serve his own kind (that is, human beings) with joy [14]. By this he becomes like God, and the commandment becomes for him not a burden but an ornament with which his soul is adorned like a heavenly bride, as St. Mar Jacob of Serugh says. 2. Many in every age exert themselves to spread the idea that God has no concern for man, as though God were busy with His heavens and man with his earth. Here the book affirms: "Their ways are before Him continually," as though what occupies the heart of God is the sons of men, for they are His creation (Ex 19:5; Deut 7:6). He looks at them in order to raise up from them saints who enjoy fellowship in glory, but those who persist in stubbornness cast themselves into eternal destruction. 3. God delights in man's giving to his brother, and so He counts almsgiving precious, like a ring that He keeps with Him, or regards it as the apple of His eye. God regards mankind, especially His saints, as the apple of His eye (Deut 32:10); He cares for them [17].

17.25.0.en: 11 And He said to them: "Beware of all unrighteousness." 12 And He gave every man commandment concerning his neighbor. 13 Their ways are before Him continually, and they are not hid from His eyes. 14 For every nation He appointed a ruler, 15 but Israel is the Lord's portion. 16 All their works are as the sun before Him, and His eyes are continually upon their ways. 17 Their iniquities are not hid from Him, but all their sins are before the Lord. 18 A man's almsgiving is as a ring with Him, and He keeps a man's kindness as the apple of His eye. 19 And afterward He will rise and repay them. He repays them their recompense upon their heads, and brings them down to the depths of the earth.

17.25.1.en: And He said to them: "Beware of all unrighteousness," and He gave every man commandment concerning his neighbor [12].

17.25.2.en: The Apostle Paul says: "And whether one member suffer, all the members suffer with it; or one member be honoured, all the members rejoice with it" (1 Cor 12:26).

17.26.0.en: v If you see a blind man falling into a pit, would you not stretch out your hand to him and support him at once? How then is it right for us to see our brothers falling into such dangers and not stretch out to them the hand of help, when they are about to fall into the everlasting pit of hell? [24]

17.26.1.en: v When you see a man in need of spiritual or bodily healing, do not say to yourself that it is the work of so-and-so to rescue him from his evil and heal him. For I am a layman and have a wife and children, and this is the work of the priests and monks. Answer me, O man: if you found a vessel full of gold, would you say to yourself: Why does not so-and-so take this vessel... Rather, you hasten like a ravening wolf and take it before any man. Let this be your longing for your fallen brothers, putting it in your mind that you have found a very precious treasure, which is your care for the matter of your brother's salvation. Behold, God Himself says by the mouth of His apostle that if you rescue a man from error you save a soul from death!

17.26.2.en: v When a thorn enters a man's heel, the whole body often feels it and cares for it. The back bends, and the belly and what is connected with them, and the two hands move like guards and servants to draw out what has entered the heel, and the head bows toward it, and the eyes watch what is happening with all care.

17.27.0.en: So although the foot is the lowest in that it is unable to rise, yet when the head bows toward it, equality between them appears, and it enjoys the same honor, especially when the foot causes the head to bow and come down to it, not as one who offers a kindness, but because of its connection with the foot... The head is crowned, and the whole body is honored. The mouth speaks and the eyes laugh and rejoice [25].

17.27.1.en: St. John Chrysostom Their ways are before Him continually, and they are not hid from His eyes [13].

17.27.2.en: v God points to the vast distance that separates us from Him. "Tell Me: who is it that tries to hide himself from Me, who know secrets precisely?!"

17.28.0.en: St. John Chrysostom v The number of souls, in our view, cannot be counted; the same applies to persons, for all of them have countless movements, behaviors, aims, feelings and sensations! There is only One who is able to govern all these in the best way of governance and lordship, for He knows the proper times, and the suitable, fitting help and when to give it, and the ways of training and guidance; He is God, the Father of the whole universe [26].

17.29.0.en: v God's providence cares for us every day, on the level of the community as in private life, in secret and in public, even when we know nothing of His dispensation [27].

17.30.0.en: v All things were created in the first place for the benefit of the rational being... God is not, as Celsus thinks, concerned only with the universe as a whole, but besides this He cares for each rational being in particular. Nevertheless His providence for the whole does not fail, for even if a part of the whole is dissolved because of the sin of the rational man, God seeks to purify it and cleanse it and restore the universe to Himself [28].

17.30.1.en: Origen He appointed a ruler for every nation, but Israel is the portion of the Lord [14].

17.30.2.en: God counted Israel as His portion, so He entered with it into a covenant, and it befits Israel to open its heart to the nations, for God Himself cares for them and appoints a ruler for every nation. If the nations rejected faith in God, God did not withdraw His care from them completely, but appointed rulers for them Himself until the King of kings should come and draw them to faith in Him.

17.31.0.en: v I say: Does God use injustice to snatch the nations from the authority of His enemies and call them to faith in Him and to submission to His authority? Not so! For Israel was once His portion (Sir 17:14). But the nations made Israel turn away from God by sin, and because of their sins God said to them: "If ye transgress, I will scatter you abroad among the nations" (Neh 1:8). But again He said to them: "But if ye turn unto me, and keep my commandments, and do them; though there were of you cast out unto the uttermost part of the heaven, yet will I gather them from thence, says the Lord" (Neh 1:9; Deut 30:4). And because the rulers of this world (Jn 16:11) first invaded the portion of the Lord, the Lord necessarily leaves the ninety and nine on the mountains (Mt 18:12; Lk 15:4-5), and comes down to the lands, and seeks the one lost sheep, and when He finds it He brings it back on His shoulders to the complete pasture on high [29].

17.31.1.en: St. John Chrysostom All their works are as the sun before Him, and His eyes are continually upon their ways [15].

17.31.2.en: Their iniquities are not hid from Him, and all their sins are before the Lord [16].

17.31.3.en: A man's almsgiving is as a seal with Him, and He keeps kindness as the apple of His eye [17].

17.31.4.en: And afterward He will rise and repay them, and recompense them according to their deserts upon their heads [18].

17.32.0.en: 20 But He made for the repentant a return, and comforted those of faint patience, and appointed for them the portion of truth. 21 So repent to the Lord, and cease from sins, 22 make supplication before His face, and lessen offenses. 23 Return to the Most High, and turn away from iniquity, and hate abomination with utmost hatred; for is there one who praises the Most High in hell? 24 Learn the commandments of God and His judgments. And be steadfast in the lot of the offering and of prayer to the Most High. 25 Enter into the inheritance of the holy age, with the living who confess to the Lord. 26 Do not linger in the error of the hypocrites. Confess before death, for confession ceases from the dead, since he returns to nothing. 27 For as long as you are alive and in health, you praise the Lord and boast of His mercies. 28 How great is the mercy of the Lord and His forgiveness for those who repent to Him. 29 Men cannot have everything, for the son of man is not immortal. 30 What is brighter than the sun? Yet even this is eclipsed, and the wicked thinks of flesh and blood. 31 The Lord reviews the hosts of the height of heaven, but men are all dust and ashes.

17.32.1.en: Repentance in its essence is a return to the divine embrace, a coming back to the Most High, and a serious longing to enjoy the pledge of heaven.

17.32.2.en: v Question: What is the difference between "godly sorrow" and "the sorrow of the world"? (2 Cor 7:10)?

17.33.0.en: Sorrow according to the will of God is that a man grieves over his neglect or contempt of God's commandment, as the Psalm says: "Zeal hath taken hold upon me because of the wicked that forsake thy law" (Ps 119:45). As for sorrow according to the will of the world, it happens if what causes it is something human or pertaining to the world [30].

17.33.1.en: v Question: What is the sorrow that we must bear in order to deserve the blessing (Mt 5:4)?!

17.34.0.en: ...when we grieve over our sins, whether because of the insult to God, since transgression of the Law dishonors God (Rom 2:23), or when we weep over those who are sinking in the danger of sin, for "the soul that sinneth, it shall die" (Ezek 18:4), imitating him who said: "I shall bewail many which have sinned already, and have not repented" (2 Cor 12:21) [31].

17.34.1.en: St. Basil the Great He makes a return for the repentant, and comforts him who lacks endurance [19].

17.34.2.en: As He speaks of the nations as those who reject the testimony of creation to the almighty, loving and wise Creator, while the Lord chose Israel as a portion for Himself, He now opens the door of hope for the nations and for Israel, declaring man's inability to act by himself. All, as sons of men, need the coming of the Lord Himself incarnate, shining with His divine light, as the Sun of Righteousness.

17.34.3.en: v Whoever sinned in his body is obliged to use the body in compensation and atonement.

17.34.4.en: You have blasphemed, so you must praise God with your mouth. You have stolen, so you must make restitution with a good deed.

17.34.5.en: You have drunk intoxicants, so you must fast. You have been proud, so you must be humble.

17.34.6.en: You have envied another, so you must pray for the one you envied.

17.34.7.en: You have perhaps killed, so you must bear the pain of martyrdom, and weary your body with mortification [32].

17.34.8.en: St. Basil the Great v Those who believe in the Lord must offer repentance according to the preaching of John and of our Lord Jesus Christ (Mt 4:17). And those who do not repent now receive a more severe punishment than those who were condemned before the time of the Gospel (Mt 11:20-21) [33].

17.34.9.en: v The present life is the time of repentance and forgiveness of sins, and in the life to come comes the time of just judgment [34].

17.34.10.en: v After departing from this life there is no opportunity for good works, for God in His longsuffering supplies us with the present life to practice the things that please Him [35].

17.34.11.en: St. Basil the Great Return to the Lord, and forsake your sins.

17.34.12.en: Pray before Him, and lessen your iniquity [20].

17.34.13.en: v Question: What are the fruits that are tested for true repentance?

17.34.14.en: Answer: The manner of those who repent, and the tendencies of those who withdraw from sin, and their struggle for the fruit worthy of repentance (Lk 3:8), which was spoken of in its own places [36] (which is returning to God) [37].

17.34.15.en: St. Basil the Great Return to the Most High, and turn away from injustice, and hate defilement intensely [21].

17.34.16.en: Who will praise the Most High in the abyss, as the living and the thankful do? [22]

17.34.17.en: Thanksgiving ceases from the dead, since he no longer lives, so none praises the Lord but the living and healthy [23].

17.34.18.en: Repentance is possible here on earth, and not in the other world.

17.34.19.en: v Let us grieve here for the one who went out of the banquet (because of his filthy garments), for there no one can grieve for his neighbor.

17.34.20.en: Let each one fear lest he be the one wearing the filthy clothes, who is driven out of the banquet.

17.34.21.en: Let each one see whether his garments are beautiful and holy, and let him whiten them if they are filthy with passions.

17.34.22.en: And if they have become filthy, let him cleanse them with repentance before the Bridegroom comes out to see the invited guests in his place.

17.34.23.en: Let each one wash his garments here in our place, for there is opportunity to cleanse them if they have become filthy.

17.34.24.en: In that place, when a man enters the banqueting couch, he is not permitted to change his filthy clothes at the banquet.

17.34.25.en: And if a man is found there wearing filthy clothes, they will cast him out, he and his clothes, to leave the banquet.

17.34.26.en: There they accept neither repentance nor petition nor supplication, for the word of the King is not resisted.

17.34.27.en: Here return is possible in all deeds, and whoever has fallen finds it easy to rise if he wishes.

17.34.28.en: And whoever was an adulterer is sanctified by repentance, and whoever was a debtor can pay his debts.

17.34.29.en: And whoever is wearing filthy clothes washes them with tears, and they become cleaner than the fire that purifies filth [38].

17.34.30.en: St. Mar Jacob of Serugh St. Augustine sees that the word "dead" here refers to the sinner, whose soul is truly dead, so he cannot offer a sacrifice of thanksgiving or praise to God, and if he offers it, it issues from his mouth and not from his heart.

17.34.31.en: v For this One who is our Head, the Savior of the body itself, cannot be carried by any bodily desire in any evil way, so that He would need to restrain His feet from it, yet they (the members of His body) can by the freedom of their will walk thus. This is what we do when we restrain our feet from evil desires, the way that He Himself does not walk, so that we do not walk in it. By this we can keep the word of God, if we do not walk after evil desires (see Sir 20:17). By this we do not seek evil desires but resist them by the Spirit who lusts against the flesh (Gal 17:5), so that they do not draw us and seduce us and cast us into evil ways.

17.34.32.en: St. Augustine David the prophet fears lest by falling into iniquity and disobedience he descend to the depths of the abyss, and it shut its mouth upon him, so that he does not return to God by repentance and become qualified to praise Him. As long as we are in the world, the abyss will not be able to shut its mouth upon us!

17.34.33.en: v "Let not the deep swallow me up, and let not the pit shut her mouth upon me" (Ps 69:25).

17.34.34.en: What does this mean? For what is he praying? The depth of human iniquity is a great abyss; whoever falls into it falls to far depths. In any case, whoever falls into it and confesses his sins to God, the depths do not shut their mouth upon him. As it is said in the Psalm: "Out of the depths have I cried unto thee, O Lord. Lord, hear my prayer" (Ps 130:1-2). But the matter is different if the disaster mentioned elsewhere in the Holy Bible concerning the sinner occurs: "When the wicked comes, contempt comes, and he falls deep into sin and disobedience" (Prov 18:3). For then the abyss shuts its mouth upon him. What does it mean that it shuts its mouth upon him? It firmly closes the mouth of the wicked. When he refuses to confess his guilt, he is in truth dead, like one who does not exist...

17.34.35.en: My brothers and sisters, let us tremble at this disaster. If you see a person committing a sin, count him or her as having fallen into the abyss. But if you point out his sin to him, and he says to you: "I am wrong. Truly I confess," then the abyss has not yet shut its mouth upon him. But if you hear him say: "Is what I am doing evil? then he has become a defender of his sin, and the abyss shuts its mouth upon him. And there is no way to draw him out of the abyss. Clearly, if he does not confess, there is no room for mercy.

17.34.36.en: If you defend your sin, will God free you from it? If you want Him to be your Deliverer, you must be the public prosecutor against yourself! [39]

17.34.37.en: St. Augustine How great is the mercy of the Lord, and He offers Himself as an atonement for those who return to Him! [24]

17.34.38.en: When man isolates himself from clinging to the Lord, he is counted as a dead man, unable to enjoy the life of praise and thanksgiving. He is counted as one who does not exist, not enjoying eternity. He is dust and ashes, but his Creator, who loves him, awaits him. Indeed, He helps him to return to Him. He is compassionate, powerful, and a lover of mankind.

17.34.39.en: The merciful God longs for man's salvation and glory more than man himself longs for his own salvation. He supports us and helps us even when we suffer from distraction of mind.

17.34.40.en: v Remember that God is gentle and tender and bears with our distraction (in prayer), and waits to grant us to pray in a perfect way. When He grants us that prayer, He accepts it from us, and does not remember how we used to pray wrongly before. If you were before a judge and while you were speaking you began to whisper with a friend, what would happen? Yet God lifts us up by prayers which other thoughts break in upon.

17.34.41.en: When you read, He speaks with you, and when you pray, you speak with Him. If this is so, shall we despair, brethren, supposing that punishment awaits one whose mind wanders distracted during his prayer? No, let us say: "Rejoice the soul of thy servant: for unto thee do I lift up my soul!"

17.34.42.en: How do I lift it up? As much as I can according to the strength that You give me; as much as I can control my scattered thoughts. For You are gentle and tender, do not drive me away. Strengthen me that I may stand, and bear with me until I attain this [40].

17.34.43.en: St. Augustine For man has not power over all things, for the son of man is not immortal [25].

17.34.44.en: What is brighter than the sun? Yet it is eclipsed; so are flesh and blood when evil is buried in the heart [26].

17.34.45.en: v Give careful attention to this matter, in order to restrain those who aim at deceiving themselves, and who have nothing to do with ascribing to creatures the honor that belongs to the Creator. Therefore the Holy Bible did not only show the beauty of the sun and its enormity and its benefits by saying: "Its rays are like the bridegroom, like the mighty man in its running in its course," but also spoke of its limitedness and weakness.

17.34.46.en: Listen to what it says in another place: "What is brighter than the sun, yet it is eclipsed" (see Sir 17:26). Do not be deceived by appearances. It tells us: if the Creator had not willed and directed it, it would disappear as if it had never existed [41].

17.34.47.en: St. John Chrysostom (The Lord) examines the powers of high heaven, but all men are dust and ashes [27].

17.34.48.en: v The heavenly beings are immortal by the goodness that is in them, but the earthly beings become mortal by their own evil will, that will which increases in the irrational through their laziness and ignorance of God [42].

17.34.49.en: v The rational man who thinks of fellowship with God and life in Him will never cling to anything base or earthly, but directs his mind toward the heavenly, eternal things, knowing that the will of God, which is the cause of every good and the source of all the blessings of men, is that men be saved [43].

17.34.50.en: St. Anthony the Great Inspired by Sirach 17

17.35.s.en: You created me and saved me and await my return to You

17.35.0.en: v My wonderful Creator and Savior.

17.35.1.en: Your wonderful love for me remains a subject of wonder to the heavenly ones.

17.35.2.en: By a word from Your mouth You created the universe; it was enough for You to say: "Let there be light..."

17.35.3.en: But as for me, You made me with Your hands from dust.

17.35.4.en: You breathed the breath of life, and behold, I am in Your image!

17.35.5.en: You clothed me with wonderful strength, and gave me authority over the earthly creatures.

17.35.6.en: You distinguished me with free will and mind and understanding; Your eye is upon me to raise up from me an ambassador for You!

17.35.7.en: v In foolishness I gave You my back, not my face.

17.35.8.en: Your image was stripped from me, and I returned to dust in corruption.

17.35.9.en: You did not leave me in my corruption, but came down to me.

17.35.10.en: And became man for my sake, to establish with me an everlasting covenant.

17.35.11.en: You gave me Your grace that I may return to You, and You establish Your Kingdom within me.

17.35.12.en: You commanded me to love You, and to love all my brothers in humanity, so that I may truly become Your ambassador, O All-Loving.

17.35.13.en: v Your eyes await my return to You, and You grant me the spirit of holiness befitting one whom You established as Your son in the waters of Baptism!

17.35.14.en: So I defy death, and set out with every morning toward the pledge of heaven!

17.35.15.en: The heavenly ones long for the day of our meeting with You face to face.

17.35.16.en: We join their ranks, and become with them a heavenly chorus ever praising!
